question.full_text:
A photon and an electron, each of $20\,\mathrm{eV}$ energy, move in free space. The ratio of linear momentum of electron $p_e$ to that of photon $p_{Ph}$, $\dfrac{p_e}{p_{Ph}}$ is : (Take speed of light $= 3 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, charge of electron $= -1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$ and mass of electron $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$ )
(1) $275$
(2) $\dfrac{2}{450}$
(3) $\dfrac{1}{250}$
(4) $225$
question.html:
A photon and an electron, each of 20 eV energy, move in free space. The ratio of linear momentum of electron pe to that of photon pPh, pepPh is : (Take speed of light = 3 × 108 m s-1, charge of electron = -1.6 × 10-19 C and mass of electron 14πε0 = 9 × 10-31 kg )
  1. (1)275
  2. (2)2450
  3. (3)1250
  4. (4)225
question.stem: A photon and an electron, each of $20\,\mathrm{eV}$ energy, move in free space. The ratio of linear momentum of electron $p_e$ to that of photon $p_{Ph}$, $\dfrac{p_e}{p_{Ph}}$ is : (Take speed of light $= 3 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, charge of electron $= -1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$ and mass of electron $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$ )

steps: $E = 20\,\mathrm{eV} = 20 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 3.2 \times 10^{-18}\,\mathrm{J}$.
For the electron (non-relativistic), $p_e = \sqrt{2mE} = \sqrt{2 \times 9 \times 10^{-31} \times 3.2 \times 10^{-18}} = \sqrt{5.76 \times 10^{-48}} = 2.4 \times 10^{-24}\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.
For the photon, $p_{Ph} = \frac{E}{c} = \frac{3.2 \times 10^{-18}}{3 \times 10^{8}} = 1.067 \times 10^{-26}\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.
$\frac{p_e}{p_{Ph}} = \frac{2.4 \times 10^{-24}}{1.067 \times 10^{-26}} = 225$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. E = 20 eV = 20 × 1.6 × 10-19 = 3.2 × 10-18 J.
  2. For the electron (non-relativistic), pe = 2mE = 2 × 9 × 10-31 × 3.2 × 10-18 = 5.76 × 10-48 = 2.4 × 10-24 kg m s-1.
  3. For the photon, pPh = Ec = 3.2 × 10-183 × 108 = 1.067 × 10-26 kg m s-1.
  4. pepPh = 2.4 × 10-241.067 × 10-26 = 225, which is option 4.

question.full_text:
Water flows in a streamline motion through a horizontal pipe of circular cross-section as shown in the figure. The pressure difference of water between $P$ and $Q$ is $15\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$. The area of cross-section at $P$ and $Q$ are $40\,\mathrm{cm^2}$ and $20\,\mathrm{cm^2}$, respectively. The rate of flow of water through the pipe, in $\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}$, is: [Take density of water $= 1000\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$]
[Figure: Horizontal pipe narrowing from a wide section P to a narrow section Q and widening again, with its axis]
(1) $400$
(2) $100$
(3) $200$
(4) $300$
question.html:
Water flows in a streamline motion through a horizontal pipe of circular cross-section as shown in the figure. The pressure difference of water between P and Q is 15 N m-2. The area of cross-section at P and Q are 40 cm2 and 20 cm2, respectively. The rate of flow of water through the pipe, in cm3 s-1, is: [Take density of water = 1000 kg m-3]
  1. (1)400
  2. (2)100
  3. (3)200
  4. (4)300
question.stem: Water flows in a streamline motion through a horizontal pipe of circular cross-section as shown in the figure. The pressure difference of water between $P$ and $Q$ is $15\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$. The area of cross-section at $P$ and $Q$ are $40\,\mathrm{cm^2}$ and $20\,\mathrm{cm^2}$, respectively. The rate of flow of water through the pipe, in $\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}$, is: [Take density of water $= 1000\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$]

figures.text: Horizontal pipe narrowing from a wide section P to a narrow section Q and widening again, with its axis

checks.print_match: not a vector figure: drawn from the spec

spec.title: Horizontal pipe narrowing from a wide section P to a narrow section Q and widening again, with its axis

steps: Continuity: $A_P v_P = A_Q v_Q \Rightarrow v_Q = \frac{40}{20} v_P = 2v_P$.
Bernoulli (horizontal pipe): $P_P - P_Q = \frac{1}{2}\rho (v_Q^2 - v_P^2) = \frac{1}{2}\rho (3v_P^2)$.
Rate of flow $= A_P v_P = 40\,\mathrm{cm^2} \times 10\,\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}} = 400\,\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Continuity: AP vP = AQ vQ ⇒ vQ = 4020 vP = 2vP.
  2. Bernoulli (horizontal pipe): PP - PQ = 12ρ (vQ2 - vP2) = 12ρ (3vP2).
  3. 15 = 12(1000)(3vP2) = 1500 vP2 ⇒ vP2 = 0.01.
  4. vP = 0.1 m s-1 = 10 cm s-1.
  5. Rate of flow = AP vP = 40 cm2 × 10 cm s-1 = 400 cm3 s-1, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Continuity gives v_Q = 2 v_P; Bernoulli 15 = (1/2)(1000)(3 v_P^2) gives v_P = 0.1 m/s, so Q = 40 cm^2 x 10 cm/s = 400 cm^3/s.

question.full_text:
A thin horizontal disc is rotating about a vertical axis passing through its fixed centre $O$. Its angular momentum is $L_A$ and $L_B$ computed about points $A$ and $B$, respectively, with $OB = 2 \times OA$. The value of $\frac{L_A}{L_B}$ is :
[Figure: Horizontal disc about centre O rotating anticlockwise, with points A and B on a dotted line from O, OB = 2 OA]
(1) $2$
(2) $\frac{1}{4}$
(3) $\frac{1}{2}$
(4) $1$
question.html:
A thin horizontal disc is rotating about a vertical axis passing through its fixed centre O. Its angular momentum is LA and LB computed about points A and B, respectively, with OB = 2 × OA. The value of LALB is :
  1. (1)2
  2. (2)14
  3. (3)12
  4. (4)1
question.stem: A thin horizontal disc is rotating about a vertical axis passing through its fixed centre $O$. Its angular momentum is $L_A$ and $L_B$ computed about points $A$ and $B$, respectively, with $OB = 2 \times OA$. The value of $\frac{L_A}{L_B}$ is :

figures.text: Horizontal disc about centre O rotating anticlockwise, with points A and B on a dotted line from O, OB = 2 OA

checks.print_match: not a vector figure: drawn from the spec

spec.title: Horizontal disc about centre O rotating anticlockwise, with points A and B on a dotted line from O, OB = 2 OA

steps: The centre $O$ (the centre of mass) is fixed, so $\vec v_{cm} = 0$ and the total linear momentum $\vec P = M\vec v_{cm} = 0$.
About any point $P$: $\vec L_P = \vec L_O + \vec r_{PO} \times \vec P$.
With $\vec P = 0$, $\vec L_A = \vec L_B = \vec L_O = I\omega$, independent of $OA$ and $OB$.
$\frac{L_A}{L_B} = 1$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. The centre O (the centre of mass) is fixed, so →vcm = 0 and the total linear momentum →P = M→vcm = 0.
  2. About any point P: →LP = →LO + →rPO × →P.
  3. With →P = 0, →LA = →LB = →LO = Iω, independent of OA and OB.
  4. LALB = 1, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Centre O is fixed so the disc's total linear momentum is zero; angular momentum is then the same about every point, so L_A/L_B = 1.

question.full_text:
Consider a long solenoid of length $l$ and radius $r$. If $n$ is the number of turns per unit length and $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space, the inductance of the solenoid is :
(1) $2\mu_0 \pi n^2 r^2 l$
(2) $\mu_0 \pi n^2 r^2 l$
(3) $\mu_0 n^2 r^2 l$
(4) $(\mu_0 / 2\pi) n^2 r^2 l$
question.html:
Consider a long solenoid of length l and radius r. If n is the number of turns per unit length and μ0 is the permeability of free space, the inductance of the solenoid is :
  1. (1)2μ0 π n2 r2 l
  2. (2)μ0 π n2 r2 l
  3. (3)μ0 n2 r2 l
  4. (4)(μ0 / 2π) n2 r2 l
question.stem: Consider a long solenoid of length $l$ and radius $r$. If $n$ is the number of turns per unit length and $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space, the inductance of the solenoid is :

steps: Field inside a long solenoid: $B = \mu_0 n I$.
Flux through one turn: $\phi = B A = \mu_0 n I \pi r^2$.
Total turns $N = n l$, so flux linkage $N\phi = \mu_0 n^2 \pi r^2 l\, I$.
$L = \frac{N\phi}{I} = \mu_0 \pi n^2 r^2 l$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Field inside a long solenoid: B = μ0 n I.
  2. Flux through one turn: φ = B A = μ0 n I π r2.
  3. Total turns N = n l, so flux linkage Nφ = μ0 n2 π r2 l  I.
  4. L = NφI = μ0 π n2 r2 l, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Self-inductance of a long solenoid L = mu0 n^2 A l with A = pi r^2, giving mu0 pi n^2 r^2 l.

question.full_text:
The temperature of a metallic sphere of radius $R$ is increased by a small amount $\Delta T$ . If the linear coefficient of thermal expansion of the metal is $\alpha$ , the approximate increase in the volume of the sphere is :
(1) $6\pi R^{3}\alpha\Delta T$
(2) $2\pi R^{3}\alpha\Delta T$
(3) $3\pi R^{3}\alpha\Delta T$
(4) $4\pi R^{3}\alpha\Delta T$
question.html:
The temperature of a metallic sphere of radius R is increased by a small amount Δ T . If the linear coefficient of thermal expansion of the metal is α , the approximate increase in the volume of the sphere is :
  1. (1)6π R3αΔ T
  2. (2)2π R3αΔ T
  3. (3)3π R3αΔ T
  4. (4)4π R3αΔ T
question.stem: The temperature of a metallic sphere of radius $R$ is increased by a small amount $\Delta T$ . If the linear coefficient of thermal expansion of the metal is $\alpha$ , the approximate increase in the volume of the sphere is :

steps: The coefficient of volume expansion is $\gamma = 3\alpha$.
The initial volume is $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}$.
$\Delta V = \gamma V \Delta T = 3\alpha \cdot \frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3} \Delta T$.
$\Delta V = 4\pi R^{3}\alpha\Delta T$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. The coefficient of volume expansion is γ = 3α.
  2. The initial volume is V = 43π R3.
  3. Δ V = γ V Δ T = 3α · 43π R3 Δ T.
  4. Δ V = 4π R3αΔ T, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Volume expansion coefficient is 3 alpha, so dV = 3 alpha x (4/3) pi R^3 x dT = 4 pi R^3 alpha dT.

question.full_text:
Consider two circuits, (A) and (B), each having two resistors. One of them has a positive temperature coefficient of resistance, $+\alpha$, while the other one has a negative temperature of coefficient, $-\alpha$, as shown in the figure. The current through these circuits are denoted by $I_A$ and $I_B$. At initial temperature, the resistance of the two resistors is $R_0$. As the temperature is increased, the correct option that describes the variation of current in these circuits is :
[Figure: Circuit (A): cell V with R0(1-αΔT) and R0(1+αΔT) in series; circuit (B): cell V with the two resistors in parallel]
(1) both $I_A$ and $I_B$ remain constant
(2) $I_A$ remains constant while $I_B$ increases
(3) $I_A$ decreases while $I_B$ increases
(4) $I_A$ increases while $I_B$ decreases
question.html:
Consider two circuits, (A) and (B), each having two resistors. One of them has a positive temperature coefficient of resistance, +α, while the other one has a negative temperature of coefficient, -α, as shown in the figure. The current through these circuits are denoted by IA and IB. At initial temperature, the resistance of the two resistors is R0. As the temperature is increased, the correct option that describes the variation of current in these circuits is :
  1. (1)both IA and IB remain constant
  2. (2)IA remains constant while IB increases
  3. (3)IA decreases while IB increases
  4. (4)IA increases while IB decreases
question.stem: Consider two circuits, (A) and (B), each having two resistors. One of them has a positive temperature coefficient of resistance, $+\alpha$, while the other one has a negative temperature of coefficient, $-\alpha$, as shown in the figure. The current through these circuits are denoted by $I_A$ and $I_B$. At initial temperature, the resistance of the two resistors is $R_0$. As the temperature is increased, the correct option that describes the variation of current in these circuits is :

figures.text: Circuit (A): cell V with R0(1-αΔT) and R0(1+αΔT) in series; circuit (B): cell V with the two resistors in parallel

checks.print_match: all 14 label(s) printed; 100% of the spec's lines on the printed ones, 100% of the printed lines covered

spec.title: Circuit (A): cell V with R0(1-αΔT) and R0(1+αΔT) in series; circuit (B): cell V with the two resistors in parallel

steps: Circuit (A) has the two resistors in series: $R_A = R_0(1-\alpha\Delta T) + R_0(1+\alpha\Delta T) = 2R_0$.
$R_A$ is independent of $\Delta T$, so $I_A = \frac{V}{2R_0}$ remains constant.
Circuit (B) has them in parallel: $R_B = \frac{R_0(1-\alpha\Delta T)\,R_0(1+\alpha\Delta T)}{2R_0} = \frac{R_0}{2}\left(1-\alpha^2\Delta T^2\right)$.
$R_B$ decreases as $\Delta T$ increases, so $I_B = \frac{V}{R_B}$ increases, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Circuit (A) has the two resistors in series: RA = R0(1-αΔ T) + R0(1+αΔ T) = 2R0.
  2. RA is independent of Δ T, so IA = V2R0 remains constant.
  3. Circuit (B) has them in parallel: RB = R0(1-αΔ T) R0(1+αΔ T)2R0 = R02(1-α2Δ T2).
  4. RB decreases as Δ T increases, so IB = VRB increases, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Series sum stays 2R0 so I_A is constant; parallel equivalent R0(1-alpha^2 dT^2)/2 decreases so I_B increases.

chapter.why: The answer depends on how resistance changes with temperature for positive and negative temperature coefficients (R = R0(1 + alpha*dT)) and how that changes the current in series/parallel combinations, which is taught in Current Electricity.

subtopics.name: Temperature Coefficient of Resistance
subtopics.why: The answer depends on how resistances with temperature coefficients +alpha and -alpha change with temperature, R = R0(1 +/- alpha*dT).

subtopics.name: Combination of Resistors
subtopics.why: Whether each circuit's current stays constant or changes depends on combining these two resistances in series (sum stays 2R0) versus parallel (equivalent resistance falls), which is the combination-of-resistors result.

step_list: Add the two series resistances in (A): R0(1-αΔT)+R0(1+αΔT)=2R0, independent of temperature, so I_A stays constant.
Form the parallel combination in (B): product/sum = R0²(1-α²ΔT²)/(2R0) = (R0/2)(1-α²ΔT²).
Notice this is less than R0/2 and shrinks further as ΔT grows (second-order term survives), so I_B increases; match to the option.
difficulty.why: Three short steps, but the two live options are separated only by a second-order algebraic point that the stem never hints at — the first-order cancellation is identical in both circuits and only the surviving α²ΔT² term in the parallel case breaks the tie, so elimination and intuition both lead straight to the wrong rival.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The unsignposted insight that (1-x)(1+x)=1-x² makes the parallel resistance fall while the series sum is exactly constant; options 3 and 4 are dead, so the whole question rests on a trap option that is the natural careless answer.

steps: At fixed frequency, the number of photons per second is $n = \frac{P}{h\nu}$, so the photocurrent $I \propto P$.
$P(t) = P_0 - kt$ decreases linearly, so $I(t)$ decreases linearly with $t$.

Linearly falling $I$ with constant $|V|$ is the pair of graphs in option $2$.
ai_solution.html:

  2. P(t) = P0 - kt decreases linearly, so I(t) decreases linearly with t.
  3. Stopping potential obeys e|V| = hν - φ, which does not depend on P, so |V| stays constant.
  4. Linearly falling I with constant |V| is the pair of graphs in option 2.
ai_solution.why: Photocurrent is proportional to intensity (power), so I falls linearly with t; stopping potential depends only on frequency, so |V| stays constant.

spec.title: Zener diode, resistor R and a cell in one loop, with points C, B, A on the top wire

steps: The Zener (C to B) and resistor $R$ (B to A) are in series across the source of magnitude $|V_i| = 5\,\mathrm{V}$.
Since $|V_i| = 5\,\mathrm{V} > |V_Z| = 3\,\mathrm{V}$, the reverse-biased ideal Zener is in breakdown, so $|V_{CB}| = 3\,\mathrm{V}$.
By KVL, $|V_{BA}| = |V_i| - |V_Z| = 5 - 3 = 2\,\mathrm{V}$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. The Zener (C to B) and resistor R (B to A) are in series across the source of magnitude |Vi| = 5 V.
  2. Since |Vi| = 5 V > |VZ| = 3 V, the reverse-biased ideal Zener is in breakdown, so |VCB| = 3 V.
  3. By KVL, |VBA| = |Vi| - |VZ| = 5 - 3 = 2 V, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Zener in reverse breakdown holds 3 V across C-B; the series resistor between B and A takes the rest, 5 - 3 = 2 V.

spec.title: Terminal velocity v against sigma/rho: a straight line rising from a point beyond 1, dotted below and solid above sigma/rho = 1

steps: At terminal velocity, weight = buoyancy + viscous drag: $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \sigma g = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho g + 6\pi \eta r v$.
$v = \frac{2 r^2 (\sigma - \rho) g}{9\eta}$.
Rewrite in terms of the ratio: $v = \frac{2 r^2 \rho g}{9\eta}\left(\frac{\sigma}{\rho} - 1\right)$, with $r$, $\rho$, $\eta$ fixed.
So $v$ is a straight line in $\sigma/\rho$ with positive slope, $v = 0$ at $\sigma/\rho = 1$ (ball only falls for $\sigma/\rho > 1$).
The graph starting at $\sigma/\rho = 1$ from $v = 0$ and rising linearly is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. At terminal velocity, weight = buoyancy + viscous drag: 43π r3 σ g = 43π r3 ρ g + 6π η r v.
  2. v = 2 r2 (σ - ρ) g9η.
  3. Rewrite in terms of the ratio: v = 2 r2 ρ g9η(σρ - 1), with r, ρ, η fixed.
  4. So v is a straight line in σ/ρ with positive slope, v = 0 at σ/ρ = 1 (ball only falls for σ/ρ > 1).
  5. The graph starting at σ/ρ = 1 from v = 0 and rising linearly is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Terminal velocity v = 2r^2(sigma - rho)g/(9 eta) = k(sigma/rho - 1): linear in sigma/rho, zero at sigma/rho = 1 and rising for sigma/rho > 1, as in option 2.

question.full_text:
Two planets $P_1$ and $P_2$ with equal mass have radii $R_1$ and $R_2$, respectively, where $R_2=\frac{R_1}{2}$. The escape speeds of $P_1$ and $P_2$ are $v_1$ and $v_2$, respectively. Then $\frac{v_2}{v_1}$ is :
(1) $2$
(2) $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
(3) $1$
(4) $\sqrt{2}$
question.html:
Two planets P1 and P2 with equal mass have radii R1 and R2, respectively, where R2=R12. The escape speeds of P1 and P2 are v1 and v2, respectively. Then v2v1 is :
  1. (1)2
  2. (2)12
  3. (3)1
  4. (4)2
question.stem: Two planets $P_1$ and $P_2$ with equal mass have radii $R_1$ and $R_2$, respectively, where $R_2=\frac{R_1}{2}$. The escape speeds of $P_1$ and $P_2$ are $v_1$ and $v_2$, respectively. Then $\frac{v_2}{v_1}$ is :

steps: Escape speed: $v = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}}$.
With equal $M$: $\frac{v_2}{v_1} = \sqrt{\frac{R_1}{R_2}}$.
$R_2 = \frac{R_1}{2}$ gives $\frac{v_2}{v_1} = \sqrt{2}$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Escape speed: v = 2GMR.
  2. With equal M: v2v1 = R1R2.
  3. R2 = R12 gives v2v1 = 2, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Escape speed v = sqrt(2GM/R); equal masses so v2/v1 = sqrt(R1/R2) = sqrt(2).

An ac voltage $V = 220\sin(2\times10^{3}t)$ Volt is applied to a series LCR circuit. Then the current amplitude in this circuit is : (Given : $L = 10\,\mathrm{mH}$, $C = 25\,\mu\mathrm{F}$, $R = 100\,\Omega$)
(1) $22.0\,\mathrm{A}$
(2) $2.2\,\mathrm{A}$
(3) $5.5\,\mathrm{A}$
(4) $11.0\,\mathrm{A}$
question.html:
An ac voltage V = 220sin(2×103t) Volt is applied to a series LCR circuit. Then the current amplitude in this circuit is : (Given : L = 10 mH, C = 25 μF, R = 100 Ω)
  1. (1)22.0 A
  2. (2)2.2 A
  3. (3)5.5 A
  4. (4)11.0 A
question.stem: An ac voltage $V = 220\sin(2\times10^{3}t)$ Volt is applied to a series LCR circuit. Then the current amplitude in this circuit is : (Given : $L = 10\,\mathrm{mH}$, $C = 25\,\mu\mathrm{F}$, $R = 100\,\Omega$)

steps: From $V = 220\sin(2\times10^{3}t)$: $V_0 = 220\,\mathrm{V}$ and $\omega = 2\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
$X_L = \omega L = 2\times10^{3} \times 10\times10^{-3} = 20\,\Omega$.
$X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{2\times10^{3} \times 25\times10^{-6}} = \frac{1}{0.05} = 20\,\Omega$.
$X_L = X_C$, so the circuit is at resonance: $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2} = R = 100\,\Omega$.
$I_0 = \frac{V_0}{Z} = \frac{220}{100} = 2.2\,\mathrm{A}$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. From V = 220sin(2×103t): V0 = 220 V and ω = 2×103 rad/s.
  2. XL = ω L = 2×103 × 10×10-3 = 20 Ω.
  3. XC = 1ω C = 12×103 × 25×10-6 = 10.05 = 20 Ω.
  4. XL = XC, so the circuit is at resonance: Z = R2 + (XL - XC)2 = R = 100 Ω.
  5. I0 = V0Z = 220100 = 2.2 A, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: X_L = X_C = 20 ohm at omega = 2000 rad/s, so the circuit is at resonance, Z = R = 100 ohm and I0 = 220/100 = 2.2 A.

The induced emf between points $a$ and $b$ for configuration $P$ is $E_P$ and that for configuration $Q$ is $E_Q$. The ratio $E_P / E_Q$ is : [Neglect the effect of mutual inductance.]
[Figure: Two identical inductors in series (P) and in parallel (Q) carrying I(t), with points a and b]
(1) $2$
(2) $1/4$
(3) $1/2$
(4) $1$
question.html:
Two identical inductors are connected in two different configurations P and Q, where a time varying current I(t) is flowing, as shown in the figure. The induced emf between points a and b for configuration P is EP and that for configuration Q is EQ. The ratio EP / EQ is : [Neglect the effect of mutual inductance.]
  1. (1)2
  2. (2)1/4
  3. (3)1/2
  4. (4)1
question.stem: Two identical inductors are connected in two different configurations $P$ and $Q$, where a time varying current $I(t)$ is flowing, as shown in the figure. The induced emf between points $a$ and $b$ for configuration $P$ is $E_P$ and that for configuration $Q$ is $E_Q$. The ratio $E_P / E_Q$ is : [Neglect the effect of mutual inductance.]

figures.text: Two identical inductors in series (P) and in parallel (Q) carrying I(t), with points a and b

checks.print_match: not a vector figure: drawn from the spec

spec.title: Two identical inductors in series (P) and in parallel (Q) carrying I(t), with points a and b

steps: From the figure, in $P$ the points $a$ and $b$ lie across only the upper inductor, which carries the full current $I(t)$.
$E_P = L\frac{dI}{dt}$.
In $Q$, $a$ and $b$ lie across the two identical inductors in parallel, so $L_{eq} = \frac{L \cdot L}{L+L} = \frac{L}{2}$, carrying total current $I(t)$.
$E_Q = \frac{L}{2}\frac{dI}{dt}$.
$\frac{E_P}{E_Q} = \frac{L}{L/2} = 2$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. From the figure, in P the points a and b lie across only the upper inductor, which carries the full current I(t).
  2. EP = LdIdt.
  3. In Q, a and b lie across the two identical inductors in parallel, so Leq = L · LL+L = L2, carrying total current I(t).
  4. EQ = L2dIdt.
  5. EPEQ = LL/2 = 2, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: In P, a-b spans one inductor carrying I so E_P = L dI/dt; in Q, a-b spans two parallel inductors (L/2) carrying I so E_Q = (L/2) dI/dt; ratio = 2.

question.stem: Three identical capacitors P, Q and S, each of the capacitance C, are connected to a battery of voltage V, as shown in the figure. If the energy stored in the capacitor P and total energy stored in the system are $U_p$ and $U_t$, respectively, then the ratio $U_p / U_t$ is :

figures.text: Capacitors P and Q in series, that pair in parallel with S, all across a battery V

checks.print_match: not a vector figure: drawn from the spec

spec.title: Capacitors P and Q in series, that pair in parallel with S, all across a battery V

steps: From the figure, $P$ and $Q$ are in series, and that branch is in parallel with $S$ across the battery $V$.
Identical capacitors in series share the voltage equally, so $V_P = V_Q = \frac{V}{2}$.
$U_p = \frac{1}{2} C \left(\frac{V}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{CV^2}{8}$.
Energy in the $P$-$Q$ branch: $U_{PQ} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{C}{2} V^2 = \frac{CV^2}{4}$.
Energy in $S$: $U_S = \frac{1}{2} C V^2$.
$\frac{U_p}{U_t} = \frac{CV^2/8}{3CV^2/4} = \frac{1}{6}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. From the figure, P and Q are in series, and that branch is in parallel with S across the battery V.
  2. Identical capacitors in series share the voltage equally, so VP = VQ = V2.
  3. Up = 12 C (V2)2 = CV28.
  4. Energy in the P-Q branch: UPQ = 12·C2 V2 = CV24.
  5. Energy in S: US = 12 C V2.
  6. Ut = CV24 + CV22 = 3CV24.
  7. UpUt = CV2/83CV2/4 = 16, which is option 1.

steps: Flux through the loop: $\phi = B A = B A_0 (1 + \sin t)$.
Induced emf: $\varepsilon = -\frac{d\phi}{dt} = -B A_0 \cos t$.
Power dissipated: $P = \frac{\varepsilon^2}{R} = \frac{B^2 A_0^2}{R} \cos^2 t$.
At $t = 0$, $P = \frac{B^2 A_0^2}{R}$ (maximum, non-zero); at $t = \frac{\pi}{2}$, $P = 0$; then $P$ rises again, and $P \ge 0$ always.

Option $1$ (monotonic rise from 0) and option $4$ (constant) are wrong; option $2$ starts at $P = 0$ (that is $\sin^2 t$); option $3$ starts at a non-zero maximum and dips to zero, so the answer is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Flux through the loop: φ = B A = B A0 (1 + sin t).
  2. Induced emf: ε = -dφdt = -B A0 cos t.
  3. Power dissipated: P = ε2R = B2 A02R cos2 t.
  4. At t = 0, P = B2 A02R (maximum, non-zero); at t = π2, P = 0; then P rises again, and P ≥ 0 always.
  5. Option 1 (monotonic rise from 0) and option 4 (constant) are wrong; option 2 starts at P = 0 (that is sin2 t); option 3 starts at a non-zero maximum and dips to zero, so the answer is option 3.
ai_solution.why: EMF = -B dA/dt = -B A0 cos t, so P = e^2/R is proportional to cos^2 t: maximum (non-zero) at t = 0, falling to zero at t = pi/2, then rising again; only option 3 starts at a non-zero maximum and dips to zero.

(1) $166\,\mathrm{J}$
(2) $41.5\,\mathrm{J}$
(3) $83\,\mathrm{J}$
(4) $124.5\,\mathrm{J}$
question.html:

  1. (1)166 J
  2. (2)41.5 J

question.stem: In an adiabatic expansion, the temperature of one mole of an ideal monatomic gas ($\gamma = 5/3$) decreases from $60\,\mathrm{K}$ to $50\,\mathrm{K}$. The work done by the gas in the process is : (Take the universal gas constant as $R = 8.3\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$)

steps: For an adiabatic process the work done by the gas is $W = \frac{nR(T_1 - T_2)}{\gamma - 1}$.
$W = \frac{83}{2/3} = 124.5\,\mathrm{J}$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. For an adiabatic process the work done by the gas is W = nR(T1 - T2)γ - 1.
  2. γ - 1 = 53 - 1 = 23.
  3. nR(T1 - T2) = 1 × 8.3 × (60 - 50) = 83 J.
  4. W = 832/3 = 124.5 J, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Adiabatic work W = nR(T1 - T2)/(gamma - 1) = 1 x 8.3 x 10 / (2/3) = 124.5 J.

question.full_text:
Consider a particle moving along a straight line, whose position as a function of time is given by $s(t) = \alpha t^{2} - \beta t + \gamma$, where $\alpha = 1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, $\beta = 6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $\gamma = 5\,\mathrm{m}$. The average speed of the particle, in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, from $t = 0$ to $t = 6\,\mathrm{s}$ is:
(1) $0$
(2) $12$
(3) $6$
(4) $3$
question.html:
Consider a particle moving along a straight line, whose position as a function of time is given by s(t) = α t2 - β t + γ, where α = 1 m s-2, β = 6 m s-1 and γ = 5 m. The average speed of the particle, in m s-1, from t = 0 to t = 6 s is:
  1. (1)0
  2. (2)12
  3. (3)6
  4. (4)3
question.stem: Consider a particle moving along a straight line, whose position as a function of time is given by $s(t) = \alpha t^{2} - \beta t + \gamma$, where $\alpha = 1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, $\beta = 6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $\gamma = 5\,\mathrm{m}$. The average speed of the particle, in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, from $t = 0$ to $t = 6\,\mathrm{s}$ is:

steps: With the given constants, $s(t) = t^{2} - 6t + 5$ (in m).
$v = \frac{ds}{dt} = 2t - 6$, which is zero at $t = 3\,\mathrm{s}$, so the particle reverses direction there.
Average speed $= \frac{18\,\mathrm{m}}{6\,\mathrm{s}} = 3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. With the given constants, s(t) = t2 - 6t + 5 (in m).
  2. v = dsdt = 2t - 6, which is zero at t = 3 s, so the particle reverses direction there.
  3. s(0) = 5 m, s(3) = 9 - 18 + 5 = -4 m, s(6) = 36 - 36 + 5 = 5 m.
  4. Distance = |s(3) - s(0)| + |s(6) - s(3)| = 9 + 9 = 18 m.
  5. Average speed = 18 m6 s = 3 m s-1, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Velocity 2t-6 reverses at t=3 s; distance = |s(3)-s(0)| + |s(6)-s(3)| = 9 + 9 = 18 m over 6 s, so average speed = 3 m/s.

question.full_text:
An ideal gas is made of polyatomic molecules. Each of the molecules has three translational, three rotational and $f$ number of vibrational modes. If the ratio of heat capacities $\frac{C_p}{C_v}$ of the gas is $\frac{8}{7}$, then the value of $f$ is:
(1) $1$
(2) $4$
(3) $3$
(4) $2$
question.html:
An ideal gas is made of polyatomic molecules. Each of the molecules has three translational, three rotational and f number of vibrational modes. If the ratio of heat capacities CpCv of the gas is 87, then the value of f is:
  1. (1)1
  2. (2)4
  3. (3)3
  4. (4)2
question.stem: An ideal gas is made of polyatomic molecules. Each of the molecules has three translational, three rotational and $f$ number of vibrational modes. If the ratio of heat capacities $\frac{C_p}{C_v}$ of the gas is $\frac{8}{7}$, then the value of $f$ is:

steps: Each translational and rotational mode contributes 1 degree of freedom; each vibrational mode contributes 2 (kinetic and potential), so $F = 3 + 3 + 2f = 6 + 2f$.
For an ideal gas $\gamma = \frac{C_p}{C_v} = 1 + \frac{2}{F}$.
$1 + \frac{2}{F} = \frac{8}{7} \Rightarrow \frac{2}{F} = \frac{1}{7} \Rightarrow F = 14$.
$6 + 2f = 14 \Rightarrow f = 4$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Each translational and rotational mode contributes 1 degree of freedom; each vibrational mode contributes 2 (kinetic and potential), so F = 3 + 3 + 2f = 6 + 2f.
  2. For an ideal gas γ = CpCv = 1 + 2F.
  3. 1 + 2F = 87 ⇒ 2F = 17 ⇒ F = 14.
  4. 6 + 2f = 14 ⇒ f = 4, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Each vibrational mode adds 2 degrees of freedom, so F = 6 + 2f; gamma = 1 + 2/F = 8/7 gives F = 14, so f = 4.

spec.title: Charged dielectric sphere of radius R with a thin tube; unit charge moved from A (2R) to B (3R)

steps: The field is conservative, so the work depends only on the end points: $W = q(V_B - V_A)$ with $q = 1$.
Total charge of the sphere: $Q = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \rho$.
Outside the sphere ($r \ge R$): $V(r) = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r} = \frac{\rho R^3}{3\epsilon_0 r}$.
At $A$ ($r = 2R$): $V_A = \frac{\rho R^2}{6\epsilon_0}$.
At $B$ ($r = 3R$): $V_B = \frac{\rho R^2}{9\epsilon_0}$.
$|W| = |V_B - V_A| = \frac{\rho R^2}{\epsilon_0}\left(\frac{1}{6} - \frac{1}{9}\right) = \frac{\rho R^2}{18\epsilon_0}$.
So $n = 18$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. The field is conservative, so the work depends only on the end points: W = q(VB - VA) with q = 1.
  2. Total charge of the sphere: Q = 43π R3 ρ.
  3. Outside the sphere (r ≥ R): V(r) = Q4πε0 r = ρ R33ε0 r.
  4. At A (r = 2R): VA = ρ R26ε0.
  5. At B (r = 3R): VB = ρ R29ε0.
  6. |W| = |VB - VA| = ρ R2ε0(16 - 19) = ρ R218ε0.
  7. So n = 18, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Work = q(V_B - V_A) with outside potential V = rho R^3/(3 eps0 r): rho R^2/eps0 (1/6 - 1/9) = rho R^2/(18 eps0), so n = 18.

Use external potential V = Q/(4πε₀r) and form V_A − V_B = Q/(4πε₀)·(1/2R − 1/3R) = Q/(24πε₀R)
Substitute Q and simplify to ρR²/(nε₀), reading off n
difficulty.why: Hard: the figure is built to make the candidate start integrating the interior field through the tube when in fact both endpoints are outside the sphere and the whole thing collapses to a two-point potential difference — that unsignposted insight, plus a four-factor algebraic chain (volume charge, 1/4πε₀, 1/6R) in which the two most common slips land exactly on options 6 and 9, puts it above a routine potential problem.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The deliberately misleading tube/figure hides the path-independence shortcut, and the distractors are precisely the results of dropping the 1/3 in the sphere volume or botching 1/2R − 1/3R, so elimination gives no help.

checks.print_match: not a vector figure: drawn from the spec

spec.title: Current I0 enters a circular loop at A and leaves at C; arcs ABC and ADC, centre O, radius r

steps: A and C are diametrically opposite, so $ABC$ and $ADC$ are semicircles in parallel.
Since $R_{ABC} = \frac{1}{2}R_{ADC}$, current divides inversely: $I_{ABC} = \frac{2I_0}{3}$, $I_{ADC} = \frac{I_0}{3}$.
Field of a semicircular arc at its centre: $B = \frac{\mu_0 i}{4r}$.
The two arcs carry current in opposite senses about $O$, so their fields oppose: $B = \frac{\mu_0}{4r}\left(\frac{2I_0}{3} - \frac{I_0}{3}\right)$.
The straight leads lie along the line through $O$, so they contribute $0$.
$B = \frac{\mu_0 I_0}{12r}$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. A and C are diametrically opposite, so ABC and ADC are semicircles in parallel.
  2. Since RABC = 12RADC, current divides inversely: IABC = 2I03, IADC = I03.
  3. Field of a semicircular arc at its centre: B = μ0 i4r.
  4. The two arcs carry current in opposite senses about O, so their fields oppose: B = μ04r(2I03 - I03).
  5. The straight leads lie along the line through O, so they contribute 0.
  6. B = μ0 I012r, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Current splits 2I0/3 in ABC and I0/3 in ADC; semicircle fields oppose, net = mu0(I0/3)/(4r) = mu0 I0/(12r); straight leads point at O and give zero.

spec.title: Bob B hanging from the ceiling by a string; point mass A moving horizontally at 10 m/s towards B

steps: In a head-on elastic collision between equal masses with B at rest, velocities are exchanged, so $v_B = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
Check whether B rises above the horizontal: $v_B^2 = 100 < 2gL = 2 \times 10 \times 10 = 200$, so B stops before the string becomes horizontal and the string stays taut.
Energy conservation: $\frac{1}{2} m v_B^2 = m g h$.
$h = \frac{v_B^2}{2g} = \frac{100}{20} = 5\,\mathrm{m}$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. In a head-on elastic collision between equal masses with B at rest, velocities are exchanged, so vB = 10 m s-1.
  2. Check whether B rises above the horizontal: vB2 = 100 < 2gL = 2 × 10 × 10 = 200, so B stops before the string becomes horizontal and the string stays taut.
  3. Energy conservation: 12 m vB2 = m g h.
  4. h = vB22g = 10020 = 5 m, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Elastic collision of equal masses transfers full velocity 10 m/s to B; since v^2 = 100 < 2gL = 200 the string stays taut and h = v^2/2g = 5 m.

question.full_text:
An electromagnetic wave travelling in a lossless dielectric medium having a dielectric constant, $\varepsilon_r = 9$, has the electric field, $E_x = E_0 \sin(kz - 2\pi \times 10^6 t)\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ where $E_0$ is the amplitude and $k$ is the wave vector. Among the following options, the incorrect choice is:
(1) The direction of propagation of the electromagnetic wave is along $+z$
(2) The speed of the electromagnetic wave inside the medium is $10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
(3) The wavelength of the electromagnetic wave inside the medium is $300\ \mathrm{m}$
(4) The magnetic field is given by the relation $B_y = \frac{B_0}{\nu} \sin(kz - 2\pi \times 10^6 t)$ where $\nu$ is the speed of the electromagnetic wave inside the medium
question.html:
An electromagnetic wave travelling in a lossless dielectric medium having a dielectric constant, εr = 9, has the electric field, Ex = E0 sin(kz - 2π × 106 t) V m-1 where E0 is the amplitude and k is the wave vector. Among the following options, the incorrect choice is:
  1. (1)The direction of propagation of the electromagnetic wave is along +z
  2. (2)The speed of the electromagnetic wave inside the medium is 108 m s-1
  3. (3)The wavelength of the electromagnetic wave inside the medium is 300 m
  4. (4)The magnetic field is given by the relation By = B0ν sin(kz - 2π × 106 t) where ν is the speed of the electromagnetic wave inside the medium
question.stem: An electromagnetic wave travelling in a lossless dielectric medium having a dielectric constant, $\varepsilon_r = 9$, has the electric field, $E_x = E_0 \sin(kz - 2\pi \times 10^6 t)\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ where $E_0$ is the amplitude and $k$ is the wave vector. Among the following options, the incorrect choice is:

options.text: The direction of propagation of the electromagnetic wave is along $+z$
The speed of the electromagnetic wave inside the medium is $10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
The wavelength of the electromagnetic wave inside the medium is $300\ \mathrm{m}$
The magnetic field is given by the relation $B_y = \frac{B_0}{\nu} \sin(kz - 2\pi \times 10^6 t)$ where $\nu$ is the speed of the electromagnetic wave inside the medium

answer.ai_text: The wavelength of the electromagnetic wave inside the medium is $300\ \mathrm{m}$

steps: The phase $kz - \omega t$ means the wave travels along $+z$, so option $1$ is correct.
With $\mu_r = 1$, $v = \frac{c}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_r}} = \frac{3\times 10^8}{\sqrt{9}} = 10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so option $2$ is correct.
$\omega = 2\pi \times 10^6\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ gives $f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} = 10^6\ \mathrm{Hz}$.
$\lambda = \frac{v}{f} = \frac{10^8}{10^6} = 100\ \mathrm{m} \neq 300\ \mathrm{m}$, so option $3$ is incorrect.
For $E$ along $x$ and propagation along $+z$, $B$ lies along $y$ with $B_y = \frac{E_0}{v}\sin(kz - \omega t)$, which option $4$ intends.
The incorrect choice is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. The phase kz - ω t means the wave travels along +z, so option 1 is correct.
  2. With μr = 1, v = cεr = 3× 1089 = 108 m s-1, so option 2 is correct.
  3. ω = 2π × 106 rad s-1 gives f = ω2π = 106 Hz.
  4. λ = vf = 108106 = 100 m ≠ 300 m, so option 3 is incorrect.
  5. For E along x and propagation along +z, B lies along y with By = E0vsin(kz - ω t), which option 4 intends.
  6. The incorrect choice is option 3.
ai_solution.why: v = c/sqrt(9) = 1e8 m/s, f = 1e6 Hz, so lambda = v/f = 100 m, not 300 m; option 3 is the incorrect statement.

question.full_text:
A particle of mass $M$ moves along a horizontal x axis from $x = 0$ to $x = L$. The coefficient of kinetic friction varies as a function of x as $\mu_k(x) = \mu_0 - \alpha x$, where $\mu_0$, $\alpha$ are constants of appropriate dimensions, so that $\mu_k(L) = 0$. The total work done by the frictional force during the motion is $n\mu_0 MgL$, where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity. The value of n is:
(1) $\frac{1}{2}$
(2) $3$
(3) $1$
(4) $\frac{1}{3}$
question.html:
A particle of mass M moves along a horizontal x axis from x = 0 to x = L. The coefficient of kinetic friction varies as a function of x as μk(x) = μ0 - α x, where μ0, α are constants of appropriate dimensions, so that μk(L) = 0. The total work done by the frictional force during the motion is nμ0 MgL, where g is the acceleration due to gravity. The value of n is:
  1. (1)12
  2. (2)3
  3. (3)1
  4. (4)13
question.stem: A particle of mass $M$ moves along a horizontal x axis from $x = 0$ to $x = L$. The coefficient of kinetic friction varies as a function of x as $\mu_k(x) = \mu_0 - \alpha x$, where $\mu_0$, $\alpha$ are constants of appropriate dimensions, so that $\mu_k(L) = 0$. The total work done by the frictional force during the motion is $n\mu_0 MgL$, where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity. The value of n is:

steps: From $\mu_k(L) = 0$: $\mu_0 - \alpha L = 0 \Rightarrow \alpha = \frac{\mu_0}{L}$.
Friction force magnitude at $x$: $f(x) = \mu_k(x) M g = (\mu_0 - \alpha x) M g$.
$|W| = \int_0^L (\mu_0 - \alpha x) M g\,dx = M g\left(\mu_0 L - \frac{\alpha L^2}{2}\right)$.
Substitute $\alpha = \frac{\mu_0}{L}$: $|W| = M g\left(\mu_0 L - \frac{\mu_0 L}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\mu_0 M g L$.
So $n = \frac{1}{2}$ (in magnitude), which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. From μk(L) = 0: μ0 - α L = 0 ⇒ α = μ0L.
  2. Friction force magnitude at x: f(x) = μk(x) M g = (μ0 - α x) M g.
  3. |W| = ∫0L (μ0 - α x) M g dx = M g(μ0 L - α L22).
  4. Substitute α = μ0L: |W| = M g(μ0 L - μ0 L2) = 12μ0 M g L.
  5. So n = 12 (in magnitude), which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Since mu_k(L)=0, alpha = mu0/L; friction work magnitude = integral of (mu0 - alpha x) M g dx from 0 to L = mu0 M g L/2, so n = 1/2.

question.stem: Consider three media $P$, $Q$ and $R$ with refractive indices $1$, $1.25$, and $1.5$, respectively. The medium $Q$ having a thickness of $5\,\mathrm{cm}$ is placed between extended media $P$ and $R$ as shown in the figure. An object $O$ is placed at the center of medium $Q$. If viewed from medium $P$ near the normal direction, the apparent depth of $O$ is $h_1$. For similar observation from medium $R$, the apparent depth is $h_2$. The value of $|h_1 - h_2|$, in cm, is:

figures.text: Medium Q of thickness 5 cm between extended media P (above) and R (below, shaded), object O at the centre of Q

checks.print_match: not a vector figure: drawn from the spec

spec.title: Medium Q of thickness 5 cm between extended media P (above) and R (below, shaded), object O at the centre of Q

steps: $O$ is at the centre of $Q$, so its real distance from each interface is $d = \frac{5}{2} = 2.5\,\mathrm{cm}$.
Viewed from $P$: $h_1 = d\,\frac{n_P}{n_Q} = 2.5 \times \frac{1}{1.25} = 2\,\mathrm{cm}$.
Viewed from $R$: $h_2 = d\,\frac{n_R}{n_Q} = 2.5 \times \frac{1.5}{1.25} = 3\,\mathrm{cm}$.
$|h_1 - h_2| = |2 - 3| = 1\,\mathrm{cm}$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. O is at the centre of Q, so its real distance from each interface is d = 52 = 2.5 cm.
  2. Viewed from P: h1 = d nPnQ = 2.5 × 11.25 = 2 cm.
  3. Viewed from R: h2 = d nRnQ = 2.5 × 1.51.25 = 3 cm.
  4. |h1 - h2| = |2 - 3| = 1 cm, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Real depth 2.5 cm each side; h1 = 2.5(1/1.25) = 2 cm, h2 = 2.5(1.5/1.25) = 3 cm, so |h1 - h2| = 1 cm.

A point charge $-q$ ($q << Q$) with mass $m$ is released from rest at a distance of $3R$ from the centre of the charged sphere. When the point charge reaches the surface of the sphere, its speed is : ($\epsilon_0$ is the permittivity of vacuum, neglect gravitational forces).
(1) $\sqrt{\dfrac{Qq}{4\pi\epsilon_0 mR}}$
(2) $\sqrt{\dfrac{3Qq}{4\pi\epsilon_0 mR}}$
(3) $\sqrt{\dfrac{2Qq}{3\pi\epsilon_0 mR}}$
(4) $\sqrt{\dfrac{Qq}{3\pi\epsilon_0 mR}}$
question.html:
Consider a fixed uniformly charged insulating sphere with radius R and total charge +Q. A point charge -q (q << Q) with mass m is released from rest at a distance of 3R from the centre of the charged sphere. When the point charge reaches the surface of the sphere, its speed is : (ε0 is the permittivity of vacuum, neglect gravitational forces).
  1. (1)Qq4πε0 mR
  2. (2)3Qq4πε0 mR
  3. (3)2Qq3πε0 mR
  4. (4)Qq3πε0 mR
question.stem: Consider a fixed uniformly charged insulating sphere with radius $R$ and total charge $+Q$. A point charge $-q$ ($q << Q$) with mass $m$ is released from rest at a distance of $3R$ from the centre of the charged sphere. When the point charge reaches the surface of the sphere, its speed is : ($\epsilon_0$ is the permittivity of vacuum, neglect gravitational forces).

steps: Outside the sphere the potential is $V(r) = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r}$, so the charge $-q$ has potential energy $U(r) = -\frac{Qq}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r}$.
Energy conservation from $r=3R$ (at rest) to $r=R$: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = U(3R) - U(R) = \frac{Qq}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left(\frac{1}{R} - \frac{1}{3R}\right)$.
$\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{Qq}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\cdot\frac{2}{3R} = \frac{Qq}{6\pi\epsilon_0 R}$.
$v^2 = \frac{Qq}{3\pi\epsilon_0 mR}$, so $v = \sqrt{\frac{Qq}{3\pi\epsilon_0 mR}}$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Outside the sphere the potential is V(r) = Q4πε0 r, so the charge -q has potential energy U(r) = -Qq4πε0 r.
  2. Energy conservation from r=3R (at rest) to r=R: 12mv2 = U(3R) - U(R) = Qq4πε0(1R - 13R).
  3. 12mv2 = Qq4πε0·23R = Qq6πε0 R.
  4. v2 = Qq3πε0 mR, so v = Qq3πε0 mR, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Energy conservation: loss in PE kQq(1/R - 1/3R) = 2kQq/(3R) equals (1/2)mv^2, giving v^2 = Qq/(3 pi eps0 m R).

question.full_text:
A car travels on a circular racetrack of radius $50\,\mathrm{m}$, which is banked at an angle $\theta$. If the car travels at a speed $10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, then the wear and tear on its tyres is minimum. Taking the acceleration due to gravity to be $10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, the value of $\theta$ is:
(1) $\tan^{-1}\left(2\sqrt{3}\right)$
(2) $\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)$
(3) $\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)$
(4) $\tan^{-1}\left(\sqrt{3}/2\right)$
question.html:
A car travels on a circular racetrack of radius 50 m, which is banked at an angle θ. If the car travels at a speed 10 m s-1, then the wear and tear on its tyres is minimum. Taking the acceleration due to gravity to be 10 m s-2, the value of θ is:
  1. (1)tan-1(23)
  2. (2)tan-1(15)
  3. (3)tan-1(25)
  4. (4)tan-1(3/2)
question.stem: A car travels on a circular racetrack of radius $50\,\mathrm{m}$, which is banked at an angle $\theta$. If the car travels at a speed $10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, then the wear and tear on its tyres is minimum. Taking the acceleration due to gravity to be $10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, the value of $\theta$ is:

steps: Minimum wear and tear means the banking alone provides the centripetal force, so friction is zero.
With no friction, $N\cos\theta = mg$ and $N\sin\theta = \frac{mv^2}{r}$, giving $\tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{rg}$.
$\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Minimum wear and tear means the banking alone provides the centripetal force, so friction is zero.
  2. With no friction, Ncosθ = mg and Nsinθ = mv2r, giving tanθ = v2rg.
  3. tanθ = (10)250 × 10 = 100500 = 15.
  4. θ = tan-1(15), which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Minimum tyre wear means no friction needed: tan(theta) = v^2/(rg) = 100/(50 x 10) = 1/5.

spec.title: Graph of P against theta: a single hump rising from zero at pi/2 and falling to zero at -pi/2

steps: The particles stay symmetric about the vertical diameter: one at angle $\theta$, the other at $\pi-\theta$.
Velocity of the clockwise particle at $\theta$: $\vec v_1 = \omega(\sin\theta, -\cos\theta)$.
Velocity of the anticlockwise particle at $\pi-\theta$: $\vec v_2 = \omega(-\sin\theta, -\cos\theta)$.
Total momentum $\vec P = m(\vec v_1 + \vec v_2) = (0, -2m\omega\cos\theta)$, so $|P| = 2m\omega|\cos\theta|$.
As $\theta$ goes from $\frac{\pi}{2}$ to $-\frac{\pi}{2}$, $|P|$ rises from $0$ to its maximum $2m\omega$ at $\theta = 0$ and falls back to $0$, an arch shape, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. The particles stay symmetric about the vertical diameter: one at angle θ, the other at π-θ.
  2. Velocity of the clockwise particle at θ: →v1 = ω(sinθ, -cosθ).
  3. Velocity of the anticlockwise particle at π-θ: →v2 = ω(-sinθ, -cosθ).
  4. Total momentum →P = m(→v1 + →v2) = (0, -2mωcosθ), so |P| = 2mω|cosθ|.
  5. As θ goes from π2 to -π2, |P| rises from 0 to its maximum 2mω at θ = 0 and falls back to 0, an arch shape, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: By symmetry the horizontal velocity components cancel and the vertical ones add, giving P = 2mv|cos θ|: zero at A and B, maximum at θ = 0, a half-sine arch.

chapter.name: Center of Mass
chapter.why: The answer turns on the total linear momentum of a two-particle system as the vector sum of the particles' momenta (equivalently M times the centre-of-mass velocity), giving P = 2mv|cos theta|, which rises from zero at A to a maximum and falls back to zero at B.

subtopics.name: Problems on Velocity, Acceleration and Force of Center of Mass
subtopics.why: The answer depends on the total linear momentum of the two-particle system, P = (sum of masses) x velocity of the centre of mass, and how it varies with theta as the particles move.

step_list: Recognise the symmetry: if one particle is at angle θ, the other (started together at π/2, opposite sense) is at π − θ, mirrored about the vertical axis.
Write each tangential velocity as a vector: ω(sin θ, −cos θ) for the clockwise particle and ω(−sin θ, −cos θ) for the counter-clockwise one.
Add them — the horizontal components cancel, leaving P = 2ω|cos θ| directed along the vertical.
Match the function 2ω|cos θ| over θ from π/2 down to −π/2 to the sketched curves: zero at both ends, maximum at θ = 0, i.e. a single arch.
difficulty.why: Hard: it takes four genuine steps — exploit the mirror symmetry to locate the second particle, write two tangential velocity vectors with correct signs, add and take the magnitude, then read the functional shape off a graph — and after all that three of the four sketches are still live, with the 'momentum is conserved so P is constant' trap (option 2) catching exactly the candidate who does no vector work at all.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The unstated point is that the wire exerts normal forces, so total linear momentum is NOT conserved; a sign error in one tangential velocity flips the cancellation from the horizontal to the vertical component and lands precisely on the inverted-arch distractor (option 3). The answer is a shape rather than a number, so there is no numerical sanity check to catch the error.

[Figure: Three diodes D1, D2, D3 with 1 kilo-ohm resistors connected across a 5 V battery]
(1) $W_2 > W_1 = W_3$
(2) $W_1 > W_2 > W_3$
(3) $W_3 = W_1 > W_2$
(4) $W_3 > W_2 > W_1$
question.html:

  2. (2)W1 > W2 > W3

question.stem: Three identical p-n junction diodes $D_1, D_2$ and $D_3$ are connected across a battery as shown in the figure. If the width of the depletion regions of $D_1, D_2$ and $D_3$ are $W_1, W_2$ and $W_3$, respectively, then the correct option is:

figures.text: Three diodes D1, D2, D3 with 1 kilo-ohm resistors connected across a 5 V battery

checks.print_match: not a vector figure: drawn from the spec

spec.title: Three diodes D1, D2, D3 with 1 kilo-ohm resistors connected across a 5 V battery

steps: The battery's long plate (positive) is on the left, so the left junction is at higher potential than the right junction.
$D_1$ points from left to right, so its anode is at the higher potential: forward biased, so $W_1$ is less than the unbiased width.
$D_3$ points from right to left, so its cathode is at the higher potential: reverse biased, so $W_3$ is greater than the unbiased width.
The branch with $D_2$ is broken (open gap), so no voltage acts on $D_2$: it is unbiased and $W_2$ keeps its equilibrium value.
Therefore $W_3 > W_2 > W_1$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. The battery's long plate (positive) is on the left, so the left junction is at higher potential than the right junction.
  2. D1 points from left to right, so its anode is at the higher potential: forward biased, so W1 is less than the unbiased width.
  3. D3 points from right to left, so its cathode is at the higher potential: reverse biased, so W3 is greater than the unbiased width.
  4. The branch with D2 is broken (open gap), so no voltage acts on D2: it is unbiased and W2 keeps its equilibrium value.
  5. Therefore W3 > W2 > W1, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: D1 is forward biased (narrowest depletion), D2 sits in an open (broken) branch so it is unbiased, and D3 is reverse biased (widest), so W3 > W2 > W1.

chapter.name: Semiconductor Electronics
chapter.why: The answer turns on how the depletion-region width of a p-n junction diode changes under forward versus reverse bias, which is semiconductor electronics.

subtopics.name: PN Junction Diode Under Reverse Bias
subtopics.why: The answer W3 > W2 > W1 rests on the depletion region widening under reverse bias (D3), so D3's is the widest, compared with the unbiased D2 in the open branch.

subtopics.name: PN Junction Diode Under Forward Bias
subtopics.why: The answer also needs the depletion region to narrow under forward bias (D1), so D1's width is the smallest; the question directly compares the two bias conditions.

step_list: Read the circuit: three parallel branches across the 5 V battery, and notice the small gap (two dots not joined) in the middle branch containing D2 — that branch is open.

Fix the bias of each diode from the arrow direction relative to the battery terminals: D1 is forward biased, D3 is reverse biased, and D2 carries no current and sits at zero applied bias (equilibrium width).
Map bias to depletion width: forward bias narrows it, zero bias leaves it at the equilibrium value, reverse bias widens it, then order W1, W2, W3.
difficulty.why: Three steps, and the options do not narrow anything — the key and its exact reversal are both on the paper, so elimination is useless and the whole question rests on two unsignposted judgements: spotting the tiny break in the middle branch and remembering which way bias moves the depletion width.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The open middle branch is a drawing detail, not stated in words; a candidate who misses it gives D2 a forward bias and the answer collapses. On top of that, the forward-narrows/reverse-widens rule is exactly the kind of fact students invert, and option 2 is built to catch that inversion.

ai_solution.html:

  2. 1v1 = 1f1 + 1u1 = 110 - 130 = 115, so v1 = +15 cm right of L1.

  5. v2 = -60 cm, i.e. 60 cm to the left of the concave lens, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: L1 forms image 15 cm right of it, i.e. virtual object 12 cm right of L2; concave lens then gives v = -60 cm, so 60 cm left of the concave lens.

question.full_text:
A solid sphere A of radius $R$ and mass $M$ is attached at a point to a smaller solid sphere B of radius $r < R$ and mass $m < M$. Assume that the line joining their centres lies along the horizontal. The moment of inertia of the system calculated about a vertical axis passing through the centre of A is $I_{A}$ and that calculated about a vertical axis passing through the centre of B is $I_{B}$. The difference $I_{A} - I_{B}$ is:
[Figure: Sphere A touching smaller sphere B; vertical axis through centre of A (I_A) and through centre of B (I_B)]
(1) $0$
(2) $(M - m)(R + r)^{2}$
(3) $(m - M)(R + r)^{2}$
(4) $(m - M)(R - r)^{2}$
question.html:
A solid sphere A of radius R and mass M is attached at a point to a smaller solid sphere B of radius r < R and mass m < M. Assume that the line joining their centres lies along the horizontal. The moment of inertia of the system calculated about a vertical axis passing through the centre of A is IA and that calculated about a vertical axis passing through the centre of B is IB. The difference IA - IB is:
  1. (1)0
  2. (2)(M - m)(R + r)2
  3. (3)(m - M)(R + r)2
  4. (4)(m - M)(R - r)2
question.stem: A solid sphere A of radius $R$ and mass $M$ is attached at a point to a smaller solid sphere B of radius $r < R$ and mass $m < M$. Assume that the line joining their centres lies along the horizontal. The moment of inertia of the system calculated about a vertical axis passing through the centre of A is $I_{A}$ and that calculated about a vertical axis passing through the centre of B is $I_{B}$. The difference $I_{A} - I_{B}$ is:

figures.text: Sphere A touching smaller sphere B; vertical axis through centre of A (I_A) and through centre of B (I_B)

checks.print_match: not a vector figure: drawn from the spec

spec.title: Sphere A touching smaller sphere B; vertical axis through centre of A (I_A) and through centre of B (I_B)

steps: The spheres touch, so the distance between their centres is $d = R + r$.
About the axis through A: $I_A = \frac{2}{5}MR^2 + \frac{2}{5}mr^2 + m(R+r)^2$ (parallel-axis theorem for B).
About the axis through B: $I_B = \frac{2}{5}MR^2 + \frac{2}{5}mr^2 + M(R+r)^2$ (parallel-axis theorem for A).
$I_A - I_B = m(R+r)^2 - M(R+r)^2 = (m - M)(R+r)^2$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. The spheres touch, so the distance between their centres is d = R + r.
  2. About the axis through A: IA = 25MR2 + 25mr2 + m(R+r)2 (parallel-axis theorem for B).
  3. About the axis through B: IB = 25MR2 + 25mr2 + M(R+r)2 (parallel-axis theorem for A).
  4. IA - IB = m(R+r)2 - M(R+r)2 = (m - M)(R+r)2, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Centres are R + r apart; the own-centre terms cancel, so I_A - I_B = m(R+r)^2 - M(R+r)^2 = (m - M)(R + r)^2.

subtopics.name: Parallel Axis and Perpendicular Axis Theorem
subtopics.why: The answer (m - M)(R + r)^2 comes from shifting each sphere's moment of inertia to the other sphere's centre with the parallel axis theorem, where the 2/5 MR^2 and 2/5 mr^2 terms cancel in the difference.

step_list: Recognise the spheres touch, so the centre-to-centre separation is R + r.
Write both moments by the parallel-axis theorem: I_A = (2/5)MR² + (2/5)mr² + m(R+r)² (B shifted) and I_B = (2/5)MR² + M(R+r)² + (2/5)mr² (A shifted).
Subtract: the two self-inertia terms cancel, leaving (m − M)(R + r)².
difficulty.why: Three short steps of parallel-axis work, but the arithmetic itself is trivial because the two (2/5)MR² and (2/5)mr² self terms cancel; what carries the question is the sign, and option 2 is the precise wrong-order result, so the candidate cannot shortcut past the subtraction.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: A pure sign trap: the key and option 2 differ only in the order of subtraction, and option 4 punishes anyone who uses R − r instead of the touching-sphere separation R + r.

source.note: Stem figure (two diagrams of spheres A and B with vertical axes I_A and I_B) sits between the stem and the options; figure_bbox covers both diagrams. Options are text only.

question.full_text:
Consider that an electron is revolving in an excited state of Hydrogen atom with velocity $\sqrt{25.6}\times 10^{5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The radius of the orbit is $x\times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}$. The value of $x$ is : (Take the mass of electron to be $9\times 10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$, charge of electron $= -1.6\times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$ and $\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} = 9\times 10^{9}\,\mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,C^{-2}}$ ]
(1) 1
(2) 4
(3) 3
(4) 2
question.html:
Consider that an electron is revolving in an excited state of Hydrogen atom with velocity 25.6× 105 m s-1. The radius of the orbit is x× 10-9 m. The value of x is : (Take the mass of electron to be 9× 10-31 kg, charge of electron = -1.6× 10-19 C and 14πε0 = 9× 109 N m2 C-2 ]
  1. (1)1
  2. (2)4
  3. (3)3
  4. (4)2
question.stem: Consider that an electron is revolving in an excited state of Hydrogen atom with velocity $\sqrt{25.6}\times 10^{5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The radius of the orbit is $x\times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}$. The value of $x$ is : (Take the mass of electron to be $9\times 10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$, charge of electron $= -1.6\times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$ and $\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} = 9\times 10^{9}\,\mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,C^{-2}}$ ]

steps: For circular motion of the electron, $\frac{mv^2}{r} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{e^2}{r^2}$.
Rearranging, $r = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{e^2}{mv^2}$.
Denominator: $mv^2 = 9\times10^{-31} \times 25.6\times10^{10} = 2.304\times10^{-19}$.
$r = \frac{2.304\times10^{-28}}{2.304\times10^{-19}} = 1\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}$, so $x = 1$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. For circular motion of the electron, mv2r = 14πε0e2r2.
  2. Rearranging, r = 14πε0e2mv2.
  3. Numerator: 9×109 × (1.6×10-19)2 = 9×109× 2.56×10-38 = 2.304×10-28.
  4. Denominator: mv2 = 9×10-31 × 25.6×1010 = 2.304×10-19.
  5. r = 2.304×10-282.304×10-19 = 1×10-9 m, so x = 1, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Coulomb force supplies centripetal force: r = ke^2/(mv^2) = (9e9 x 2.56e-38)/(9e-31 x 25.6e10) = 1e-9 m, so x = 1.

subtopics.why: The answer comes from the Bohr-orbit balance of Coulomb force and centripetal force, r = ke^2/(mv^2) = 1e-9 m, which is taught under Bohr's atomic model.

step_list: Recognise that for the orbiting electron the Coulomb attraction supplies the centripetal force: mv^2/r = ke^2/r^2, so r = ke^2/(mv^2)
Square the given velocity: v^2 = 25.6 x 10^10 = 2.56 x 10^11 m^2 s^-2

difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The velocity is deliberately disguised as sqrt(25.6) x 10^5 so the square must be formed carefully (2.56 x 10^11, not 2.56 x 10^10 or 10^12); a one-decade slip or the energy-versus-force factor of two lands on a different integer option, and the integer options themselves offer no order-of-magnitude discrimination.

question.full_text:
The mean free path of molecules in an ideal gas A is half that of another ideal gas B. The diameter of the spherical molecules of gas A is twice the diameter of the molecules of B. If number densities of the gases A and B are $n_A$ and $n_B$, respectively, then the correct option is :
(1) $n_A = \frac{1}{2}n_B$
(2) $n_A = n_B$
(3) $n_A = 2n_B$
(4) $n_A = \frac{1}{4}n_B$
question.html:
The mean free path of molecules in an ideal gas A is half that of another ideal gas B. The diameter of the spherical molecules of gas A is twice the diameter of the molecules of B. If number densities of the gases A and B are nA and nB, respectively, then the correct option is :
  1. (1)nA = 12nB
  2. (2)nA = nB
  3. (3)nA = 2nB
  4. (4)nA = 14nB
question.stem: The mean free path of molecules in an ideal gas A is half that of another ideal gas B. The diameter of the spherical molecules of gas A is twice the diameter of the molecules of B. If number densities of the gases A and B are $n_A$ and $n_B$, respectively, then the correct option is :

steps: Mean free path: $\lambda = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\,\pi d^2 n}$.
Ratio: $\frac{\lambda_A}{\lambda_B} = \frac{n_B d_B^2}{n_A d_A^2}$.
With $d_A = 2d_B$: $\frac{\lambda_A}{\lambda_B} = \frac{n_B}{4 n_A}$.
Given $\frac{\lambda_A}{\lambda_B} = \frac{1}{2}$: $\frac{n_B}{4n_A} = \frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow n_A = \frac{1}{2} n_B$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Mean free path: λ = 12 π d2 n.
  2. Ratio: λAλB = nB dB2nA dA2.
  3. With dA = 2dB: λAλB = nB4 nA.
  4. Given λAλB = 12: nB4nA = 12 ⇒ nA = 12 nB, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Mean free path is proportional to 1/(n d^2); lambda_A/lambda_B = n_B d_B^2/(n_A d_A^2) = n_B/(4 n_A) = 1/2 gives n_A = n_B/2.

question.full_text:
A cylindrical cork of uniform density floats in a liquid of density $\rho_1$. If the cork is depressed slightly and released, it oscillates harmonically with time period $T$. If the same cork floats in another liquid of density $\rho_2$, then the similar oscillation has time period $2T$. The value of $\rho_2/\rho_1$ is :
(1) $\frac{1}{4}$
(2) $4$
(3) $2$
(4) $\frac{1}{2}$
question.html:
A cylindrical cork of uniform density floats in a liquid of density ρ1. If the cork is depressed slightly and released, it oscillates harmonically with time period T. If the same cork floats in another liquid of density ρ2, then the similar oscillation has time period 2T. The value of ρ2/ρ1 is :
  1. (1)14
  2. (2)4
  3. (3)2
  4. (4)12
question.stem: A cylindrical cork of uniform density floats in a liquid of density $\rho_1$. If the cork is depressed slightly and released, it oscillates harmonically with time period $T$. If the same cork floats in another liquid of density $\rho_2$, then the similar oscillation has time period $2T$. The value of $\rho_2/\rho_1$ is :

steps: For a depression $x$, the extra buoyant force is the restoring force: $F = -\rho A g x$.
So $k = \rho A g$ and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{\rho A g}}$, giving $T \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{\rho}}$ (same cork, so $m$ and $A$ are fixed).
$\frac{T_2}{T_1} = \sqrt{\frac{\rho_1}{\rho_2}} = 2$.
$\frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1} = \frac{1}{4}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. For a depression x, the extra buoyant force is the restoring force: F = -ρ A g x.
  2. So k = ρ A g and T = 2πmρ A g, giving T ∝ 1ρ (same cork, so m and A are fixed).
  3. T2T1 = ρ1ρ2 = 2.
  4. ρ2ρ1 = 14, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Restoring force rho*A*g*x gives T = 2*pi*sqrt(m/(rho*A*g)), so T is proportional to 1/sqrt(rho); doubling T means rho2 = rho1/4.

question.full_text:
For sound waves, if the number of nodes for the $5^{\mathrm{th}}$ harmonic of an open-ended pipe is $n$ and that for the $9^{\mathrm{th}}$ harmonic of the same pipe with one of its ends closed is $m$, the ratio $\frac{n}{m}$ is :
(1) $\frac{3}{5}$
(2) $\frac{5}{9}$
(3) $\frac{9}{5}$
(4) $1$
question.html:
For sound waves, if the number of nodes for the 5th harmonic of an open-ended pipe is n and that for the 9th harmonic of the same pipe with one of its ends closed is m, the ratio nm is :
  1. (1)35
  2. (2)59
  3. (3)95
  4. (4)1
question.stem: For sound waves, if the number of nodes for the $5^{\mathrm{th}}$ harmonic of an open-ended pipe is $n$ and that for the $9^{\mathrm{th}}$ harmonic of the same pipe with one of its ends closed is $m$, the ratio $\frac{n}{m}$ is :

steps: For an open pipe the $p^{\text{th}}$ harmonic has $L = p\frac{\lambda}{2}$ with antinodes at both ends, giving $p$ nodes.
So for the $5^{\text{th}}$ harmonic of the open pipe, $n = 5$.
For a closed pipe $L = (2k-1)\frac{\lambda}{4}$, with a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, giving $k$ nodes.
The $9^{\text{th}}$ harmonic means $2k-1 = 9$, so $k = 5$ and $m = 5$.
$\frac{n}{m} = \frac{5}{5} = 1$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. For an open pipe the pth harmonic has L = pλ2 with antinodes at both ends, giving p nodes.
  2. So for the 5th harmonic of the open pipe, n = 5.
  3. For a closed pipe L = (2k-1)λ4, with a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, giving k nodes.
  4. The 9th harmonic means 2k-1 = 9, so k = 5 and m = 5.
  5. nm = 55 = 1, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Open pipe pth harmonic has p nodes, so n = 5; closed pipe (2k-1)th harmonic has k nodes, so 9th harmonic has m = 5; n/m = 1.

step_list: For an open-open pipe, the 5th harmonic means L = 5λ/2, so count the nodes: 5 nodes (n = 5).
For a closed pipe only odd harmonics exist; the 9th harmonic means L = 9λ/4, so count nodes from the closed end at 0, λ/2, λ, 3λ/2, 2λ → 5 nodes (m = 5).
Form n/m.
difficulty.why: Short to execute — two node counts and a ratio — but it is not easy, because the plausible-looking 5/9 sits right next to the key and only the explicit node counting in the closed pipe (where the 9th harmonic has (9+1)/2 = 5 nodes, not 9) separates them.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The trap is treating 'harmonic number' as 'number of nodes'; the closed-pipe odd-harmonic numbering is not signposted in the stem and must be supplied by the candidate.

Consider the following nuclear reaction : $\mathrm{^{238}U \rightarrow {}^{234}Th + {}^{4}He}$ Take masses of $\mathrm{^{238}U}$, $\mathrm{^{234}Th}$ and $\mathrm{^{4}He}$ as $238.050\,\mathrm{u}$, $234.043\,\mathrm{u}$ and $4.003\,\mathrm{u}$, respectively. The Q value for the reaction, in keV, is : [Given : $1\,\mathrm{u} = 931.5\,\mathrm{MeV}\,c^{-2}$]
(1) $3740$
(2) $3726$
(3) $3730$
(4) $3736$
question.html:
Consider the following nuclear reaction : 238U → 234Th + 4He Take masses of 238U, 234Th and 4He as 238.050 u, 234.043 u and 4.003 u, respectively. The Q value for the reaction, in keV, is : [Given : 1 u = 931.5 MeV c-2]
  1. (1)3740
  2. (2)3726
  3. (3)3730

question.stem: Consider the following nuclear reaction : $\mathrm{^{238}U \rightarrow {}^{234}Th + {}^{4}He}$ Take masses of $\mathrm{^{238}U}$, $\mathrm{^{234}Th}$ and $\mathrm{^{4}He}$ as $238.050\,\mathrm{u}$, $234.043\,\mathrm{u}$ and $4.003\,\mathrm{u}$, respectively. The Q value for the reaction, in keV, is : [Given : $1\,\mathrm{u} = 931.5\,\mathrm{MeV}\,c^{-2}$]

steps: $Q = \Delta m \times 931.5\,\mathrm{MeV/u} = 0.004 \times 931.5 = 3.726\,\mathrm{MeV}$.
$3.726\,\mathrm{MeV} = 3726\,\mathrm{keV}$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Δ m = mU - (mTh + mHe) = 238.050 - (234.043 + 4.003) u.
  2. Δ m = 238.050 - 238.046 = 0.004 u.
  3. Q = Δ m × 931.5 MeV/u = 0.004 × 931.5 = 3.726 MeV.
  4. 3.726 MeV = 3726 keV, which is option 2.

question.full_text:
In a solar system, the time-period of revolution of a planet tracing a circular orbit of radius $R$ is proportional to:
(1) $R^{3}$
(2) $R^{1/2}$
(3) $R^{3/2}$
(4) $R^{2}$
question.html:
In a solar system, the time-period of revolution of a planet tracing a circular orbit of radius R is proportional to:
  1. (1)R3
  2. (2)R1/2
  3. (3)R3/2
  4. (4)R2
question.stem: In a solar system, the time-period of revolution of a planet tracing a circular orbit of radius $R$ is proportional to:

steps: Gravity provides the centripetal force: $\frac{GMm}{R^2} = m\omega^2 R = m\frac{4\pi^2}{T^2}R$.
Rearranging gives $T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM}R^3$.
Hence $T \propto R^{3/2}$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Gravity provides the centripetal force: GMmR2 = mω2 R = m4π2T2R.
  2. Rearranging gives T2 = 4π2GMR3.
  3. Hence T ∝ R3/2, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Kepler's third law: T^2 is proportional to R^3, so T is proportional to R^(3/2).

question.full_text:
Consider that $\sigma_s, k_B, b$ represent Stefan-Boltzmann constant, Boltzmann constant and Wien's displacement law constant, respectively. The dimension of $\sigma_s k_B^{-1} b$ is:
(1) $[L^{-1}T^{-1}K^{-4}]$
(2) $[L^{-1}T^{-1}K^{-2}]$
(3) $[L^{-1}K^{-2}]$
(4) $[L^{-1}T^{-1}K^{-3}]$
question.html:
Consider that σs, kB, b represent Stefan-Boltzmann constant, Boltzmann constant and Wien's displacement law constant, respectively. The dimension of σs kB-1 b is:
  1. (1)[L-1T-1K-4]
  2. (2)[L-1T-1K-2]
  3. (3)[L-1K-2]
  4. (4)[L-1T-1K-3]
question.stem: Consider that $\sigma_s, k_B, b$ represent Stefan-Boltzmann constant, Boltzmann constant and Wien's displacement law constant, respectively. The dimension of $\sigma_s k_B^{-1} b$ is:

steps: $\sigma_s = \frac{P}{A T^4} \Rightarrow [\sigma_s] = \frac{[M L^2 T^{-3}]}{[L^2][K^4]} = [M T^{-3} K^{-4}]$.
$b = \lambda_m T \Rightarrow [b] = [L K]$.
ai_solution.html:
1. σs = PA T4 ⇒ [σs] = [M L2 T-3][L2][K4] = [M T-3 K-4].
  2. kB = ET ⇒ [kB] = [M L2 T-2 K-1], so [kB-1] = [M-1 L-2 T2 K].
  3. b = λm T ⇒ [b] = [L K].

question.full_text:
A ray of light with wavelength $\lambda$ is incident on three different photo-electric cells namely 1, 2 and 3. The threshold wavelength of these photo-electric cells are $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2$ and $\lambda_3$, respectively and the magnitude of stopping potentials of these cells are $V_1$, $V_2$ and $V_3$, respectively. The relation between $\lambda$ and threshold wavelengths are $\lambda_1 < \lambda$, $\lambda_2 > \lambda$ and $\lambda_3 >> \lambda$. The correct option is:
(1) $V_1 < V_2, V_3 = 0$
(2) $V_1 = 0, V_2 < V_3$
(3) $V_1 = 0, V_2 > V_3$
(4) $V_1 > V_2, V_3 = 0$
question.html:
A ray of light with wavelength λ is incident on three different photo-electric cells namely 1, 2 and 3. The threshold wavelength of these photo-electric cells are λ1, λ2 and λ3, respectively and the magnitude of stopping potentials of these cells are V1, V2 and V3, respectively. The relation between λ and threshold wavelengths are λ1 < λ, λ2 > λ and λ3 >> λ. The correct option is:
  1. (1)V1 < V2, V3 = 0
  2. (2)V1 = 0, V2 < V3
  3. (3)V1 = 0, V2 > V3
  4. (4)V1 > V2, V3 = 0
question.stem: A ray of light with wavelength $\lambda$ is incident on three different photo-electric cells namely 1, 2 and 3. The threshold wavelength of these photo-electric cells are $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2$ and $\lambda_3$, respectively and the magnitude of stopping potentials of these cells are $V_1$, $V_2$ and $V_3$, respectively. The relation between $\lambda$ and threshold wavelengths are $\lambda_1 < \lambda$, $\lambda_2 > \lambda$ and $\lambda_3 >> \lambda$. The correct option is:

steps: Photoemission happens only if $\lambda < \lambda_{th}$. For cell 1, $\lambda_1 < \lambda$, so there is no emission and $V_1 = 0$.
For cells 2 and 3, $eV_i = hc\left(\frac{1}{\lambda} - \frac{1}{\lambda_i}\right)$.
$\lambda_3 \gg \lambda$ and $\lambda_2 > \lambda$ (with $\lambda_3 > \lambda_2$), so $\frac{1}{\lambda_3} < \frac{1}{\lambda_2}$ and therefore $V_3 > V_2$.
$V_1 = 0,\ V_2 < V_3$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Photoemission happens only if λ < λth. For cell 1, λ1 < λ, so there is no emission and V1 = 0.
  2. For cells 2 and 3, eVi = hc(1λ - 1λi).
  3. λ3 ≫ λ and λ2 > λ (with λ3 > λ2), so 1λ3 < 1λ2 and therefore V3 > V2.
  4. V1 = 0, V2 < V3, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Cell 1 has lambda1 < lambda, so there is no emission and V1 = 0; eV = hc(1/lambda - 1/lambda_th) is larger for the larger threshold, so V2 < V3.

question.full_text:
One main scale division of a Vernier calliper is equal to $1\,\mathrm{mm}$ and the number of divisions on the Vernier scale is 10. When both the jaws touch each other, the Vernier scale shifts to the left of zero of the main scale in such a way that $4^{\mathrm{th}}$ Vernier division coincides with a division of the main scale. If this Vernier caliper measures the length of a wire to be $1\,\mathrm{cm}$, the actual length of the wire is:
(1) $1.04\,\mathrm{cm}$
(2) $0.60\,\mathrm{cm}$
(3) $0.96\,\mathrm{cm}$
(4) $1.00\,\mathrm{cm}$
question.html:
One main scale division of a Vernier calliper is equal to 1 mm and the number of divisions on the Vernier scale is 10. When both the jaws touch each other, the Vernier scale shifts to the left of zero of the main scale in such a way that 4th Vernier division coincides with a division of the main scale. If this Vernier caliper measures the length of a wire to be 1 cm, the actual length of the wire is:
  1. (1)1.04 cm
  2. (2)0.60 cm
  3. (3)0.96 cm
  4. (4)1.00 cm
question.stem: One main scale division of a Vernier calliper is equal to $1\,\mathrm{mm}$ and the number of divisions on the Vernier scale is 10. When both the jaws touch each other, the Vernier scale shifts to the left of zero of the main scale in such a way that $4^{\mathrm{th}}$ Vernier division coincides with a division of the main scale. If this Vernier caliper measures the length of a wire to be $1\,\mathrm{cm}$, the actual length of the wire is:

steps: Least count $= \frac{1\,\mathrm{mm}}{10} = 0.1\,\mathrm{mm}$.
Vernier zero lies to the left of main-scale zero, so the zero error is negative.
Taking the coinciding division directly, zero error $= -4 \times 0.1\,\mathrm{mm} = -0.04\,\mathrm{cm}$.
Actual length $=$ measured $-$ zero error $= 1.00 - (-0.04) = 1.04\,\mathrm{cm}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Least count = 1 mm10 = 0.1 mm.
  2. Vernier zero lies to the left of main-scale zero, so the zero error is negative.
  3. Taking the coinciding division directly, zero error = -4 × 0.1 mm = -0.04 cm.
  4. Actual length = measured - zero error = 1.00 - (-0.04) = 1.04 cm, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: LC = 0.1 mm; Vernier zero left of main zero gives a negative zero error taken as -4 x 0.1 mm = -0.04 cm, so actual = 1 - (-0.04) = 1.04 cm.

Consider points A, B and C as shown in the figure, where the magnitudes of the electric fields are $E_A$, $E_B$ and $E_C$, respectively. spec.title: Conducting sphere with an off-centre cavity holding charge Q; point A in the cavity, points C and B outside on a line through the centre

steps: Point A lies inside the cavity alongside $Q$, where the field due to $Q$ and the induced $-Q$ on the cavity wall does not vanish, so $E_A \neq 0$.
Charge $+Q$ is induced on the outer surface; the conductor shields the cavity, so this charge spreads uniformly over the outer sphere.
Outside the sphere $E = \frac{kQ}{r^2}$ measured from the centre; since $r_B = r_C$, $E_B = E_C$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Point A lies inside the cavity alongside Q, where the field due to Q and the induced -Q on the cavity wall does not vanish, so EA ≠ 0.
  2. Charge +Q is induced on the outer surface; the conductor shields the cavity, so this charge spreads uniformly over the outer sphere.
  3. Outside the sphere E = kQr2 measured from the centre; since rB = rC, EB = EC, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: A lies inside the cavity with Q, so E_A is nonzero; the outer surface carries +Q spread uniformly (shielding), so outside fields depend only on distance from the centre, giving E_B = E_C.

In Geiger-Marsden experiment, the number of scattered $\alpha$-particles $N(\theta)$ is plotted as a function of scattering angle $\theta$. Which of the following options represents the correct plot?
(1) [Figure: N(θ) on a log scale against θ from 0 to 180 degrees: a broad hump peaking near 90°]
(2) [Figure: Option (2): log-scale N(θ) rising as a straight line with scattering angle θ]
(3) [Figure: N(theta) on a log scale versus scattering angle theta: flat near 10^7 up to about 60 degrees, then falling to about 10^3 near 175 degrees]
(4) [Figure: N(θ) on a log scale against scattering angle θ: steep fall from 10^7 near 0° flattening to about 10^2 by 180°]

spec.title: N(θ) on a log scale against scattering angle θ: steep fall from 10^7 near 0° flattening to about 10^2 by 180°

steps: Rutherford scattering formula: $N(\theta) \propto \frac{1}{\sin^4(\theta/2)}$.
As $\theta \to 0$, $\sin(\theta/2) \to 0$, so $N(\theta)$ is very large; most $\alpha$-particles pass almost undeflected.

$N(\theta)$ decreases monotonically with $\theta$; $\frac{N(10^\circ)}{N(180^\circ)} = \frac{1}{\sin^4 5^\circ} \approx 1.7\times 10^4$, and most of this fall happens at small angles, so the curve drops steeply then levels off.

Options 1 (peak at $90^\circ$) and 2 (increasing) are wrong; option 3 stays nearly flat at small angles, contrary to the formula; option 4 shows the steep fall and flat tail, so the answer is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Rutherford scattering formula: N(θ) ∝ 1sin4(θ/2).
  2. As θ → 0, sin(θ/2) → 0, so N(θ) is very large; most α-particles pass almost undeflected.
  3. N(θ) decreases monotonically with θ; N(10°)N(180°) = 1sin4 5° ≈ 1.7× 104, and most of this fall happens at small angles, so the curve drops steeply then levels off.
  4. Options 1 (peak at 90°) and 2 (increasing) are wrong; option 3 stays nearly flat at small angles, contrary to the formula; option 4 shows the steep fall and flat tail, so the answer is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Rutherford scattering gives N(theta) proportional to 1/sin^4(theta/2): a very large count at small angles that falls steeply and then levels off at a small value towards 180 degrees, as in NCERT Fig. 12.3, which is option 4.

[ $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity and $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space.]
(1) $\dfrac{4\mu_0 I^2}{\pi\lambda g}$
(2) $\dfrac{\mu_0 I^2}{2\pi\lambda g}$
(3) $\dfrac{\mu_0 I^2}{\pi\lambda g}$

Two infinitely long parallel conducting wires A and B carry currents I and 2I, respectively, in the same direction. The wire A has uniform mass per unit length λ and lies on an insulated floor. The wire B is kept fixed at a height h above the floor. The minimum magnitude of h so that the wire A does not rise from the floor is :
[ g is the acceleration due to gravity and μ0 is the permeability of free space.]
  1. (1)4μ0 I2πλ g
  2. (2)μ0 I22πλ g
  3. (3)μ0 I2πλ g

question.stem:
Two infinitely long parallel conducting wires $A$ and $B$ carry currents $I$ and $2I$, respectively, in the same direction. The wire $A$ has uniform mass per unit length $\lambda$ and lies on an insulated floor. The wire $B$ is kept fixed at a height $h$ above the floor. The minimum magnitude of $h$ so that the wire $A$ does not rise from the floor is :
[ $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity and $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space.]

steps: Currents in the same direction attract, so wire $B$ above pulls wire $A$ upward.
Force per unit length on $A$: $\frac{F}{L} = \frac{\mu_0 I (2I)}{2\pi h} = \frac{\mu_0 I^2}{\pi h}$.
Weight per unit length of $A$ is $\lambda g$; $A$ does not rise if $\frac{\mu_0 I^2}{\pi h} \le \lambda g$.
$h \ge \frac{\mu_0 I^2}{\pi \lambda g}$, so $h_{min} = \frac{\mu_0 I^2}{\pi \lambda g}$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Currents in the same direction attract, so wire B above pulls wire A upward.
  2. Force per unit length on A: FL = μ0 I (2I)2π h = μ0 I2π h.
  3. Weight per unit length of A is λ g; A does not rise if μ0 I2π h ≤ λ g.
  4. h ≥ μ0 I2π λ g, so hmin = μ0 I2π λ g, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Parallel currents attract, so B pulls A upward with force per length mu0(I)(2I)/(2 pi h) = mu0 I^2/(pi h); A stays down if this is at most lambda g, giving h_min = mu0 I^2/(pi lambda g).
